Monheim, Germany/St. Louis, USA, September 9, 2026 – Bayer and Neste, the world’s leading producer of renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel, have finalized a commercial agreement to jointly scale Bayer’s newgold® winter canola.

The collaboration will enable Bayer to significantly expand acres of winter canola in the Southern Great Plains of the US, strengthening the oilseed supply potential of lower-carbon-intensity feedstocks to meet the growing global demand for biofuels such as renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel, which is estimated to increase almost threefold reaching approximately 40 billion gallons by 2040.1,2 The high protein meal from the winter canola grain will be sold into the feed market, offering additional feed sources for dairy and beef cattle, poultry and swine markets.

“In times of geopolitical tensions, the need for more energy security and resilience while decarbonizing the transportation sector leads to growing demand for renewable fuel. This agreement further underscores Bayer’s commitment to help scale biofuels production,” said Frank Terhorst, Head of Strategy and Sustainability for Bayer’s Crop Science division. “We see the Southern Great Plains as an untapped opportunity for winter canola. The launch of newgold® winter canola will provide farmers with a profitable rotational crop with wheat and improve land utilization, while offering the opportunity to participate in a growing biofuels market.”

Bayer and Neste are establishing a newgold® network with additional value chain partners, to support the expansion of winter canola and ensure an additional market for farmers.

“Maximizing the contribution of novel types of raw materials to support growth in renewables requires open supply chain collaboration. By building robust value chains, we can turn agricultural innovations into scalable realities for growers and energy markets. Through the Bayer newgold® winter canola collaboration, we are establishing a value chain in one of Neste’s key markets and developing opportunities to increase farm yields and grower income. This renewable raw material can be scaled rapidly in the coming years, which can help meet increasing biofuels demand,” says Artturi Mikkola, Senior Vice President, Renewable Products Feedstock Sourcing and Trading at Neste.

Bayer aims to launch newgold® winter canola hybrids in the fall of 2027. These hybrids offer farmers several benefits, including winter-hardiness, TruFlex®, Bayer’s second-generation Roundup Ready trait technology, and pod shatter resistance technology. Together, these advancements can deliver strong potential for yield performance and higher oil content. TruFlex winter canola, sold under the newgold® seed brand, will be designed with the goal of acting as a new profit opportunity for the Southern Great Plains, giving growers the flexibility to decide how and where it fits best in their operation.

Biofuels can play a key role in helping the transportation sector in its energy transition since electrification may not be feasible in all transportation systems like aviation, rail, heavy duty equipment or marine. Biofuels can be produced from renewable organic materials like corn, soy, canola and other intermediate oilseed crops, such as winter canola. Bayer recently presented its biofuels platform at its investor day in Huxley, IA, where it highlighted its emergent, but leading portfolio of intermediate biofuel crops, including camelina, winter canola and CoverCress™.

It accounted for 81% of the feedstock mix for reported EU sustainable aviation fuel in 2024, according to EASA. Renewable diesel producers also buy these oils and fats.

The EU minimum share of sustainable aviation fuel rises from 2% in 2025 to 6% in 2030. If collection cannot expand as quickly, aviation producers will need to buy feedstock that already has another customer.

More sustainable fuel for aircraft can therefore mean less feedstock available for road fuels. The additional climate benefit depends partly on what replaces those road fuels.

Electrification can reduce that competition. Each road application that switches successfully to electricity reduces demand for fuel molecules, leaving more feedstock available for uses with fewer practical alternatives.

Long distance aviation needs high onboard energy density. Deep sea shipping needs low emission fuels, with options including methanol and carbon-free ammonia. Organic chemicals still require carbon atoms when their process heat is electrified.

Prioritising these applications also requires reducing their demand for new resources. More efficient aircraft and ships consume less fuel. Reuse and recycling reduce the chemical industry's need for new carbon.

Capturing biogenic CO₂ and converting it with renewable hydrogen can produce additional methanol from an existing carbon stream. The electricity requirement and the carbon's alternative use determine whether that route delivers a worthwhile climate benefit.

A fuel mandate creates a buyer. Expanding sustainable supply requires additional collection, new conversion routes and less demand from applications that can use electricity directly.

New Delhi [India], September 9 (ANI): Akasa Air on September 8 successfully operated a commercial flight using conventional aviation turbine fuel blended with 1 per cent sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), supplied by Bharat Petroleum Corporation Limited (BPCL), the airline said in a statement.

As per the release, the flight departed Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International Airport, Mumbai, at 13:05hrs IST and arrived at Manohar International Airport (GOX), Goa, at 14:30hrs IST.

"The initiative builds on the Memorandum of Understanding signed by Akasa Air and BPCL in July 2026 to explore adoption of SAF, along with other opportunities supporting aviation decarbonisation," Akasa Air noted adding, the flight will offer both the organisations with insights and practical learnings that can help inform future initiatives.

Under the MoU, both the companies agreed to establish a framework for the supply and offtake of Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF)-blended Aviation Turbine Fuel (ATF) at designated airports across India.

Commenting on the development, Ankur Goel, Chief Financial Officer, Akasa Air, said, "Sustainability is one of Akasa Air's core values and shapes how we are building the airline for the long term. Since inception, we have invested in next-generation aircraft, technology and responsible practices that enable more conscious and efficient operations, both on the ground and in the air. This flight with BPCL translates our partnership into tangible action. Scaling SAF in India will require coordinated action across the ecosystem, supported by domestic supply, enabling policy and commercial viability. We are committed to exploring this transition."

The airline is continuing to implement initiatives aimed at promoting more sustainable and efficient operations, it noted in the release adding, its Boeing 737 MAX fleet forms a key part of its efforts to operate an environmentally progressive and fuel-efficient fleet.

"Powered by CFM International LEAP-1B engines and incorporating advanced-technology winglets, the 737 MAX offers excellent economics, reducing fuel use and emissions by 20 per cent compared to the airplanes it replaces," it said.

Additionally, the airline has also partnered with OpenAirlines to deploy SkyBreathe, a fuel-management solution that uses advanced analytics to improve operational efficiency and reduce carbon emissions across its network. Akasa Air was also the first Indian airline to voluntarily discontinue traditional water-cannon salutes during route inaugurations, helping conserve more than 5.5 lakh litres of water to date.

Subhankar Sen, Director (Marketing), Bharat Petroleum Corporation Limited (BPCL), said, "The transition from conventional fuels to sustainable alternatives is both an environmental imperative and a strategic necessity for India. While feedstock availability and aggregation have historically posed challenges due to fragmented supply chains, sustained efforts across the value chain have helped create the foundation for a viable Sustainable Aviation Fuel ecosystem. BPCL remains firmly committed to advancing sustainable fuels as part of India's broader energy transition journey. As a nation that relies significantly on crude oil imports, enhancing energy security through sustainable and indigenous energy solutions is the way forward." (ANI)

The IRS on Tuesday announced regulatory guidance for the Clean Fuel Production Tax Credit’s carbon accounting that affirmed many key provisions biogas producers had hoped to see. While the agency still needs to finalize the credit’s language, the announcement provides certainty for the biogas industry.

The guidance incorporates specific credit pathways for dairy and swine manure, food waste and other organic materials. The IRS also provided assurance that the guidance would cover clean fuels produced in 2025.

While the credit has been available since 2025, many biogas producers had waited to claim it until they saw this guidance, according to Patrick Serfass, executive director of the American Biogas Council.

Dive Insight:

The credit, known in the tax code as 45Z, has faced a long regulatory road even as other credits introduced by the Inflation Reduction Act have come and gone. Notably, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act of 2025 curtailed some of the IRA’s more expansive support for fuels like hydrogen at the same time that it extended 45Z.

Tuesday’s announcement drew praise from the American Biogas Council, which has long urged federal officials to finalize 45Z language. Serfass issued a statement praising the IRS for incorporating many of the ABC’s priorities in its new guidance.

“The wait is over. Since Congress created 45Z four years ago, the biogas industry has been waiting for the certainty needed to fully put this tax credit to work,” Serfass said.

The credit was initially set to include projects producing fuels through 2027, but it was extended last year through 2029. Biogas project owners have largely held off on claiming 45Z due to uncertainty about its applicability, though there have been some exceptions.

The ABC has long contended that billions of dollars in investment were waiting on the sideline until the final credit language is adopted. Serfass said the new guidance provides enough certainty that biogas developers can incorporate its backing into future project plans for the first time.

“America produces enormous quantities of manure, food waste and other organic materials every day. Instead of wasting those resources, biogas systems can recycle them into domestic renewable energy while supporting farms, rural communities and American jobs,” he said. “Today’s action gives our industry an important new tool to build more of those projects.”

In a statement, IRS CEO Frank Bisignano said he also expects this guidance to unlock new investment, as well as strengthen domestic biofuel production and lower fuel costs.

“Today’s guidance helps America’s farmers, ranchers, and fuel producers access growing opportunities in the domestic biofuels market,” he said.

The credit was written to provide support for non-fossil transportation fuels that are below a certain carbon intensity level. The value of the credit is determined by such fuels’ carbon intensity, as calculated by a model developed by the U.S. Department of Agriculture.

The credit covers a variety of fuels beyond renewable natural gas, including ethanol, biodiesel, hydrogen and sustainable aviation fuel. The base credit as laid out in the IRA provided 20 cents per gallon multiplied by a fuel’s carbon intensity, or 35 cents per gallon if the fuel was for aviation.

In June, the USDA released an update to its model calculating emissions for certain alternative fuels, though it did not separate out manure calculations. The IRS update on Tuesday said the agency will allow the use of separate carbon intensities for different forms of manure, such as poultry or beef. The agency said it expects the USDA to provide those specific rates later this year.

The IRS will also allow transportation fuel derived from animal manure to calculate a negative emissions rate, a policy that has drawn fire from environmental groups when implemented in other clean fuels policies. And the agency will exclude from calculations the emissions attributed to indirect land use change, which has similarly come under scrutiny as the production of fuel crops has grown.

The IRS guidance also allows fuel derived from feedstocks produced in Canada or Mexico to count toward the credit; the OBBBA had limited credits for certain foreign-produced feedstocks or parts.

text:
Mitsui Mining & Smelting Co. agreed with Australian clean-energy technology developer Wildfire Energy to jointly advance a demonstration project to produce lower-cost bio-methanol from biomass and waste, with a potential future pathway to sustainable aviation fuel, the Japanese company said on September 9.

The project will be supported by an A$3.15 million grant from the Australian Renewable Energy Agency, or ARENA, and funding from Mitsui Mining & Smelting. ARENA announced the grant on July 6. The grant is equivalent to about ¥360 million ($2.34 million).

The partners plan to combine Wildfire Energy's Moving Injection Horizontal Gasification, or MIHG, technology with Mitsui Mining & Smelting's methanol-synthesis technology in a modular process designed to convert biomass and waste into biofuels at lower cost.

The work is scheduled to run from 2026 through the end of 2028 and comprises pilot testing and a feasibility study. In the pilot phase, Wildfire Energy's gasification plant will be connected to a methanol-synthesis unit being developed by Mitsui Mining & Smelting. The companies will test bio-methanol production using multiple feedstocks.

The feasibility study will assess the economic viability and environmental suitability of a process to produce bio-methanol in Queensland from more than 200,000 metric tons of waste annually. It will also examine upgrading bio-methanol into sustainable aviation fuel, the company said.

Wildfire Energy is based in Brisbane and develops technologies that convert waste and biomass into renewable energy and fuels. Its MIHG process gasifies biomass and municipal solid waste into synthesis gas without requiring feedstock pre-treatment or sorting, according to the release.

Mitsui Mining & Smelting has developed a membrane-reactor technology with EseP Co., a company based in Kyoto Prefecture, combining porous ceramic separation membranes with catalysts for methanol synthesis. The technology is designed to increase methanol yield and eliminate the recycling of unreacted gas required in conventional process designs, the company said.

Sustainable aviation fuel is an aviation fuel produced from non-fossil feedstocks and is intended to reduce lifecycle emissions compared with conventional jet fuel. The Queensland study will evaluate a potential route from waste-derived bio-methanol to that fuel category.

Exchange rate: US$1 = ¥154.

text:
Partnership aims to grow winter canola acres and renewable fuel supplies

Bayer and Neste have entered into a commercial agreement aimed at expanding winter canola production in the Southern Great Plains region of the United States. The collaboration is designed to help meet rising demand for renewable fuels while creating new market opportunities for farmers.

The agreement focuses on increasing the acreage of Bayer's newgold® winter canola, a crop expected to play an important role in the future biofuels supply chain. As governments, businesses, and industries seek lower-carbon energy sources, renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel are becoming increasingly important. Industry estimates suggest that global demand for these fuels could grow significantly over the coming decades.

Winter canola offers several advantages for both farmers and energy producers. The crop can be planted as a rotational option alongside wheat, helping diversify farm operations and improve land use efficiency. By introducing winter canola into existing farming systems, growers may have additional opportunities to increase revenue while maintaining productive agricultural land.

The partnership also supports the development of a reliable supply of oilseed feedstocks for renewable fuel production. Oil extracted from canola can be used to produce renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel. At the same time, the high-protein meal remaining after oil extraction can be used as livestock feed for dairy cattle, beef cattle, poultry, and swine.

Another important aspect of collaboration is the creation of a broader value chain network. Bayer and Neste plan to work with additional partners throughout the agricultural and energy sectors to encourage production, processing, transportation, and marketing opportunities. Building a strong supply chain can help ensure demand for growers while supporting the expansion of renewable fuel markets.

“Maximizing the contribution of novel types of raw materials to support growth in renewables requires open supply chain collaboration. By building robust value chains, we can turn agricultural innovations into scalable realities for growers and energy markets,” said Artturi Mikkola, Senior Vice President, Renewable Products Feedstock Sourcing and Trading at Neste.

HE added, “Through the Bayer newgold® winter canola collaboration, we are establishing a value chain in one of Neste’s key markets and developing opportunities to increase farm yields and grower income. This renewable raw material can be scaled rapidly in the coming years, which can help meet increasing biofuels demand.

Energy security and sustainability continue to be major priorities in many parts of the world. Renewable fuels are viewed as one practical solution for reducing emissions in transportation sectors where full electrification may be difficult. Industries such as aviation, rail transportation, marine shipping, and heavy-duty equipment often require alternative energy solutions that can work alongside existing infrastructure.

To support these growing needs, Bayer is developing new canola hybrids designed specifically for the Southern Great Plains. The company plans to introduce newgold® winter canola hybrids beginning in 2027. These hybrids are expected to offer several agronomic benefits, including improved winter hardiness, enhanced yield potential, and increased oil content.

The new canola varieties will also feature advanced trait technologies intended to help growers manage production challenges more effectively. Improved crop performance can contribute to better profitability while supporting sustainable farming practices.

For farmers, the expansion of winter canola may provide additional flexibility in crop planning. Rotational cropping systems are often used to improve soil health, manage production risks, and diversify income sources. Introducing another profitable crop option can help strengthen farm businesses while contributing to broader agricultural sustainability goals.

The growing interest in biofuels is creating opportunities across the agricultural sector. Crops such as canola, soybean, corn, and other oilseeds are increasingly being considered important components of renewable energy production. As demand rises, partnerships between agriculture and energy companies are expected to play a key role in building reliable feedstock supplies.

Industry leaders believe collaboration throughout the supply chain will be essential to achieving long-term growth. By connecting seed technology, crop production, processing infrastructure, and fuel manufacturing, stakeholders can help create a more sustainable and resilient energy future.

The Bayer and Neste agreement highlight how innovation in agriculture can contribute to renewable energy development while supporting farmers with new market opportunities. As biofuel demand continues to increase, winter canola could become an important crop for producers looking to participate in emerging energy markets.

text:
Green hydrogen research and development (R&D) projects have been included in the Netherlands’ final, EU-approved €661m ($769m) Covid recovery package.

The cash, approved under the NextGenerationEU Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF), follows the country submitting its final payment request on 2 July and will bring its total received from the fund to €3.73bn ($4.34bn).

The European Commission’s positive assessment of the request allows innovation- and education-focused initiatives advancing the adoption of green hydrogen to be eligible for a piece of the funding.

It remains unclear exactly how much of the payment could reach green hydrogen R&D, as renewable energy, energy efficiency, and tax reforms are also entitled to funds.

With the RRF set to close at the end of the year, it will be the Netherlands’ final boost from the mechanism.

The EU also recently signed off three significant Dutch state aid schemes: a $780m ($908m) initiative supporting up to 400MW of electrolysis, a €290m ($338m) hydrogen-based sustainable aviation fuel (e-SAF) scheme, and a €103 (€120m) clean maritime fuels investment.

Netherlands is positioned as a leader in hydrogen R&D in Europe, particularly as the host of the Netherlands Organisation for Scientific Research’s (TNO) Faraday Laboratory, a facility with a core focus on electrolyser technologies.

A strong network of universities, technology suppliers, and industrial users gives the country an important role within the EU’s wider push to achieve and retain technological leadership in hydrogen.

Bayer and Neste, the world’s leading producer of renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel, have finalized a commercial agreement to jointly scale Bayer’s newgold® winter canola.

The collaboration will enable Bayer to significantly expand acres of winter canola in the Southern Great Plains of the US, strengthening the oilseed supply potential of lower-carbon-intensity feedstocks to meet the growing global demand for biofuels such as renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel, which is estimated to increase almost threefold reaching approximately 40 billion gallons by 2040.1,2 The high protein meal from the winter canola grain will be sold into the feed market, offering additional feed sources for dairy and beef cattle, poultry and swine markets.

“In times of geopolitical tensions, the need for more energy security and resilience while decarbonizing the transportation sector leads to growing demand for renewable fuel. This agreement further underscores Bayer’s commitment to help scale biofuels production,” said Frank Terhorst, Head of Strategy and Sustainability for Bayer’s Crop Science division. “We see the Southern Great Plains as an untapped opportunity for winter canola. The launch of newgold® winter canola will provide farmers with a profitable rotational crop with wheat and improve land utilization, while offering the opportunity to participate in a growing biofuels market.”

Bayer and Neste are establishing a newgold® network with additional value chain partners, to support the expansion of winter canola and ensure an additional market for farmers.

“Maximizing the contribution of novel types of raw materials to support growth in renewables requires open supply chain collaboration. By building robust value chains, we can turn agricultural innovations into scalable realities for growers and energy markets. Through the Bayer newgold® winter canola collaboration, we are establishing a value chain in one of Neste’s key markets and developing opportunities to increase farm yields and grower income. This renewable raw material can be scaled rapidly in the coming years, which can help meet increasing biofuels demand,” says Artturi Mikkola, Senior Vice President, Renewable Products Feedstock Sourcing and Trading at Neste.

Bayer aims to launch newgold® winter canola hybrids in the fall of 2027. These hybrids offer farmers several benefits, including winter-hardiness, TruFlex®, Bayer’s second-generation Roundup Ready trait technology, and pod shatter resistance technology. Together, these advancements can deliver strong potential for yield performance and higher oil content. Biofuels can be produced from renewable organic materials like corn, soy, canola and other intermediate oilseed crops, such as winter canola. Bayer recently presented its biofuels platform at its investor day in Huxley, IA, where it highlighted its emergent, but leading portfolio of intermediate biofuel crops, including camelina, winter canola and CoverCress™.

title: Biofuels Market Outlook: 5 Trends Shaping Q4 2026 and 2027 - ResourceWise
description:
What does that mean for the biofuels market in Q4 2026?
Those were among the major themes discussed during ResourceWise's latest Biofuels Market Outlook webinar.
Why Could Biofuel Demand Strengthen in Q4 2026?
Current market fundamentals point toward a strong Q4 2026 compliance environment, while higher mandates create the potential for an even stronger biofuels demand outlook in 2027.
Get the Full Biofuels Market Outlook with On-Demand Webinar These elements represent only part of the market picture discussed during ResourceWise's latest Biofuels Market Outlook webinar.
text:
Biofuel markets are heading into the final quarter of 2026 with several forces pointing in the same direction: tight diesel supply, rising compliance requirements and increasingly interconnected global trade flows.

What does that mean for the biofuels market in Q4 2026? ResourceWise expects a strong Q4 compliance environment as markets work to meet rising mandates and make up for demand that was deferred earlier in the year.

In the US, high capacity utilization and imports may be needed to balance demand. Meanwhile, developments in Europe and Asia continue to reshape global biofuel and feedstock trade.

Those were among the major themes discussed during ResourceWise's latest Biofuels Market Outlook webinar.

Key Takeaways

1. Why Could Biofuel Demand Strengthen in Q4 2026?

Some biofuel demand that might otherwise have occurred earlier in 2026 has effectively been pushed into Q4. The result is an added demand already created by rising mandates.

One important factor is the continued strength of the global diesel market. Tight diesel supply has supported high diesel prices. In turn, this provides a strong price floor for biodiesel, renewable diesel, and sustainable aviation fuel (SAF).

That environment has also helped support biofuel producer margins. During the webinar, we highlighted the combination of tight conventional diesel markets and aggressive mandate growth as two important factors supporting the market through the remainder of the year.

But there is another layer to the Q4 outlook: catch-up demand.

In Europe, record heat and low rainfall pushed the Rhine to exceptionally low water levels during the summer. That made it significantly more expensive, and in some cases impossible, to move biofuels by barge from coastal production and import hubs to inland blending locations.

Read More: Record Low Rhine Water Levels Are Disrupting Europe's Biofuel Market

The result was disruption to biofuel blending and softer-than-expected demand during Q3. That demand does not necessarily disappear. Instead, some of it may move forward.

For obligated parties that still need to satisfy annual requirements, lower blending earlier in the year can mean additional volumes must be secured later. This creates the potential for Q4 compliance demand to arrive on top of an already supportive underlying market.

2. Can US Biofuel Supply Keep Pace With Demand?

The US biofuels industry may need to operate near full capacity, while imports of both biofuels and potentially feedstocks could also be needed to balance demand.

The US market illustrates just how tight the supply-demand equation could become.

ResourceWise expects the industry to need capacity utilization levels close to full through the remainder of 2026. At the same time, producers face an interesting economic decision: supplying a tight domestic market is not always necessarily the most profitable option.

US producers can manufacture fuel for domestic consumption and generate Renewable Identification Numbers (RINs). But they can also export fuel if overseas economics are sufficiently attractive, retiring the associated RINs in the process.

That means a tight domestic market does not automatically guarantee that every available gallon remains in the United States. Despite that dynamic, the broader conclusion remains the same: the US market needs substantial supply to balance its requirements.

Imports could therefore play an important role. The US will likely require biofuel imports and potentially additional feedstock imports as the market works to satisfy 2026 demand.

And the challenge does not end on December 31.

Demand requirements are set even higher for 2027, increasing the importance of production capacity, feedstock availability, and international trade as the market moves into the next compliance year.

3. Why Are Global Biofuel Trade Flows Becoming More Important?

Biofuel and feedstock markets are increasingly interconnected, meaning a supply, demand or policy change in one region can quickly influence market conditions elsewhere.

Consider the existing flow of fuels and feedstocks around the world:

The US imports feedstocks from Asia and Europe.

Europe imports renewable diesel from the US and feedstocks from Asia.

The US also imports biodiesel from Europe.

At the same time, markets including Canada, Asia and South America are developing their own demand profiles.

As domestic demand grows in those markets, volumes previously available for export may become less available to buyers elsewhere. That can alter arbitrage opportunities and put additional pressure on supply chains serving Europe and North America.

4. How Could Chinese SAF Supply Affect the European Market?

SAF provides another clear example. Growing Chinese SAF production could maintain pressure on European SAF prices as additional supply competes for demand created by Europe's aviation fuel mandates.

Chinese SAF currently faces a different European customs and trade environment than road-use HVO. As discussed during the webinar, Chinese SAF has been entering the European market in meaningful volumes.

China has substantial production capacity but comparatively limited domestic SAF demand. Additional Chinese capacity is also expected to come online.

That creates a relatively straightforward market dynamic: more supply is looking for a home.

Europe is an obvious destination. But the region's ability to absorb additional SAF remains influenced by the pace of mandated demand growth. If supply grows faster than consumption requirements, imported Chinese volumes could continue to put pressure on European SAF pricing.

This is also a useful illustration of why analyzing biofuel markets in isolation is becoming increasingly difficult.

Capacity additions in China can influence SAF pricing in Europe. European demand can affect feedstock availability elsewhere. US export economics can influence domestic RIN generation. New demand in emerging markets can reduce volumes available for established trade routes.

5. What Does the Biofuels Outlook Look Like for 2027?

Current market fundamentals point toward a strong Q4 2026 compliance environment, while higher mandates create the potential for an even stronger biofuels demand outlook in 2027.

Three factors are particularly important heading into the end of the year:

Strong diesel pricing and demand

Strong biofuel demand and pricing

Compliance shortfalls that may still need to be addressed before year-end

Together, those dynamics create a supportive setup for Q4.

But 2027 adds another consideration: mandates generally continue to increase. That means the market will need to find additional biofuel supply and the feedstocks necessary to produce it. Producers, traders, and obligated parties will also need to understand how changing regional economics affect where those volumes ultimately move.

The exact diesel-market backdrop may change, but the structural growth in mandated biofuel demand remains an important part of the equation.

The full presentation examines the global supply-demand balance in greater detail, including developments across Europe and the United States, SAF, maritime biofuels and emerging renewable fuels.

text:
Bayer and Neste are establishing a newgold® network with additional value chain partners, to support the expansion of winter canola and ensure an additional market for farmers.

“Maximizing the contribution of novel types of raw materials to support growth in renewables requires open supply chain collaboration. By building robust value chains, we can turn agricultural innovations into scalable realities for growers and energy markets. Through the Bayer newgold® winter canola collaboration, we are establishing a value chain in one of Neste’s key markets and developing opportunities to increase farm yields and grower income. This renewable raw material can be scaled rapidly in the coming years, which can help meet increasing biofuels demand,” says Artturi Mikkola, Senior Vice President, Renewable Products Feedstock Sourcing and Trading at Neste.

Bayer aims to launch newgold® winter canola hybrids in the fall of 2027. These hybrids offer farmers several benefits, including winter-hardiness, TruFlex®, Bayer’s second-generation Roundup Ready trait technology, and pod shatter resistance technology. Together, these advancements can deliver strong potential for yield performance and higher oil content. TruFlex winter canola, sold under the newgold® seed brand, will be designed with the goal of acting as a new profit opportunity for the Southern Great Plains, giving growers the flexibility to decide how and where it fits best in their operation.

Biofuels can play a key role in helping the transportation sector in its energy transition since electrification may not be feasible in all transportation systems like aviation, rail, heavy duty equipment or marine. Biofuels can be produced from renewable organic materials like corn, soy, canola and other intermediate oilseed crops, such as winter canola. Bayer recently presented its biofuels platform at its investor day in Huxley, IA, where it highlighted its emergent, but leading portfolio of intermediate biofuel crops, including camelina, winter canola and CoverCress™.
